content.comment_body: I'm experiencing a similar issue. My [product_name] with [article_no] was communicating with another [product_name] with [version_no], but suddenly the first device stopped working. I can still connect to the second device, but not the malfunctioning one. Firmware is at [version_no], and the LEDs show steady status: RX/TX is orange and LINK is green, even without a network cable. The device no longer responds to pings from my computer, but the program runs when using the SD card. Is there anything I can try at this point? Could it be a replaceable network component on the PCB, or is it likely the microcontroller is damaged? Thanks, [user_name]

Perhaps the device has frozen. Save your original program (if it's only saved to the SD card, remove it), then fully delete the configuration on the device and transfer the program again from scratch, or try uploading a simple test program.

Hi, I've performed a complete reset using the device's display, but the problem persists. As soon as the device powers up, the green link LED stays illuminated—even without a network cable attached. Neither my computer nor my network switch recognizes a connection; their LEDs remain off. I suspect a hardware defect. If so, is repair possible? Are any circuit diagrams available that could help me identify faulty components? BR [user_name]

In summary: repair is unlikely. You might be able to source a replacement network chip, but the complex soldering on SMD parts makes success uncertain. In most cases, purchasing a new device is more straightforward and cost-effective.

That's a disappointing response. A device designed for network connections fails simply by plugging in a cable, and the solution is to buy another one. These [article_no] devices cost over €170 on the secondhand market. While that cost might be manageable for a company, it's significant for a home user. Could someone clarify what to check? Is the network chip part of the processor, or a separate unit? The only chip I see on the network lines is a shunt from WE-Midcom [article_no].

I've never encountered a device failing just from connecting a network cable. The only exception would be using PoE, which is unsupported. Purchasing secondhand units is risky because their history is unknown, and for €170 you could buy a new device and upgrade your [product_name] software to the latest version free of charge. Regarding the Ethernet chip, it's likely a standard Broadcom model, definitely not part of the CPU—but you'd have to inspect the internals yourself. [company_name] does not reveal technical specifics. After checking the CPU datasheet, the Ethernet controller is integrated into the CPU. Unfortunately, this makes repairs impossible. Best regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

analysis.insight_summary: Forum participants report sudden hardware failure on [product_name] ([article_no]), which loses network connectivity as shown by constant LED status regardless of cable connection. Attempted resets and reprogramming via device interface and SD card have no effect. The likely cause is internal hardware damage, potentially to a CPU-integrated Ethernet controller, making user repair impractical. The situation leads to frustration, especially for home users facing high replacement costs and lacking detailed guidance or schematics from [company_name].
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect durable and reliable network communication from their devices, as well as the ability to diagnose and repair network hardware faults with accessible technical documentation. More support and cost-effective repair options are desired when facing hardware failure.
